newsitem.title: USA: Cash still flowing to players in Simpson case.
newsitem.headline: Cash still flowing to players in Simpson case.

text.p: Lawyers signed million-dollar books deals, a house guest became a radio talk-show host and one ex-juror even posed nude for Playboy magazine -- all thanks to their involvement in the O.J. Simpson murder trial.

Nearly one year after Simpson's acquittal on criminal charges and only days before the start of his civil trial, the cash is still flowing to just about anyone who played a major role in the last year's sensational double-murder trial.
Giving credence to pop artist Andy Warhol's prediction that everyone eventually has 15 minutes of fame, even the bit players in the case have had a chance to turn a profit.

How else would Tracy Hampton, a young woman excused from the Simpson jury in mid-trial because of illness, have been offered a Playboy spread? How else would Hank Goldberg, a junior member of the prosecution team who handled only a small portion of the case, have won a book contract?

Perhaps the least likely instant celebrity to emerge from the trial was Kato Kaelin, a struggling actor who was Simpson's house guest in June 1994 when the football star's former wife and her friend were stabbed to death. Kaelin's quirky appearance on the witness stand and his surfer-dude good looks briefly earned him his own talk show on a Los Angeles radio station and offers of small movie parts.
It remains to be seen if players in Simpson's civil trial, due to get underway next Tuesday, can expect similiar money-making opportunities.

Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki is a no-nonsense jurist who has barred television cameras from the courtroom and has already issued a sweeping "gag order" against lawyers and witnesses. Under these circumstances, it will be hard for the trial's participants to have the kind of celebrity status of many in the criminal trial, which was broadcast on television.
Prosecutors Marcia Clark and Christopher Darden did not let the fact that they lost the case prevent them from signing up with Hollywood talent agency William Morris to write books.

Darden, who is reportedly making at least $1.3 million on his book "In Contempt," made a surprisingly big splash with an autobiographical account that sold hundreds of thousands of copies and spent months on the New York Times bestseller list. He also has a movie about the trial in the works.
Clark, with whom Darden was linked romantically in the tabloid press, has also turned a devastating trial loss into gold. Her book deal is reportedly worth $4.2 million.
Simpson's lawyers have found ways of capitalising on their fame as well. Lead defence attorney Johnnie Cochran's upcoming book is expected to earn him millions of dollars.
Then there were the jurors who wrote books to explain why it took them less than three hours to reach not-guilty verdicts after nine months of often-complicated testimony.
Simpson attacked publisher Michael Viner in a recent interview in Esquire magazine, saying, "Every time (he) puts out an O.J. book, he makes money. ... Michael Viner is a new kind of pimp."

But since his acquittal last Oct. 3 in the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, Simpson has also tried to cash in on his notoriety, making paid speeches and releasing a $29.99 video telling his side of the story.
